ai-at-work.title: 4 days left: How TechCrunch Founder Summit helps you make more useful connections to scale
ai-at-work.excerpt: On November 4 at Boston’s SoWa Power Station, get ready for a full day packed with meaningful networking opportunities, actionable insights, and connections that could change the trajectory of your id
ai-at-work.dwp_take: TechCrunch is running a one-day founder summit in Boston on November 4 with networking sessions and talks aimed at helping startup founders scale their ideas. For digital workplace folks, this matters because the networking formats and connection strategies they're showcasing are exactly what most corporate intranets are desperately trying and failing to replicate. Here's the thing though: a physical event with real coffee and conversation does more for human connection in eight hours than your enterprise collaboration platform has done in eight months.

ai-at-work.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
ai-at-work.excerpt: Big Tech is pouring billions into AI infrastructure, but mounting debt, negative cash flow, and growing investor skepticism are raising questions about the sustainability of the AI spending boom.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Companies like OpenAI, Meta, and Google have spent billions on AI infrastructure while burning cash and accumulating debt, prompting investors to finally ask if this emperor has any clothes. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because those AI tools your CEO is mandating might come from vendors who are one funding round away from pivoting or shutting down. The AI gold rush has been fun to watch, but anyone betting their workplace strategy on unproven business models should probably keep their resume updated.

ai-at-work.title: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
ai-at-work.excerpt: The artificial intelligence buildout is making an enormous bet on what businesses will eventually be willing to pay for intelligence. In our research this summer on forecasting the AI bubble, we argue
ai-at-work.dwp_take:
Here's my take:

Enterprise AI vendors are betting that companies will actually pay enough money to justify the massive infrastructure costs they're pouring into building these systems. This matters because your executives are probably already asking you to justify AI investments, and the entire industry's financial model depends on proving ROI actually exists and isn't just another shiny object. The real test isn't whether AI works, it's whether it works well enough to justify the bill, and right now nobody's actually proven that at scale yet.

ai-at-work.title: Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard
ai-at-work.excerpt: Google LLC, Microsoft Corp., Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to support an upcoming website crawling standard. The technology will enable website operators to block artificial
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI are backing a new standard that lets websites block AI companies from scraping their content for training data. This matters because digital workplace teams managing internal content, documentation, and knowledge bases suddenly have a legitimate tool to prevent their carefully crafted materials from becoming someone else's AI fuel. The cynic in me notes that these same companies probably lobbied hard against regulation, so offering a technical opt-out is basically saying "we'll let you say no, but we're counting on most of you not knowing this exists."

digital-culture.title: Could AI give older creatives a second act?
digital-culture.excerpt: Advertising is made for the young by the young. That’s conventional wisdom backed up by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which in 2025 reported the median age of ad industry workers was 39, compared to
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company reports that advertising skews young in both workforce age and creative targeting, with median ad industry worker age at 39 versus 42 overall, while only 5-10% of ad budgets aim at older consumers. This matters to digital workplace leaders because age diversity directly impacts innovation, audience understanding, and whether your workplace actually reflects the customers you're trying to reach. AI tools could level the playing field for experienced creatives, but only if companies stop treating anyone over 45 like they're still learning VCR programming.

digital-culture.title: Employee engagement in U.S. hits lowest point in 15 years
digital-culture.excerpt: Worker engagement in the U.S. has dropped below 30%, to its lowest level since 2011, Gallup reports. Engagement dropped two points from last quarter, equivalent to roughly 3.2 million fewer engaged wo
digital-culture.dwp_take: Employee engagement in the U.S. just hit 30%, its worst mark since 2011, with remote workers taking the biggest hit and actively disengaged employees climbing to 18%. This matters because your beautiful intranet, your collaboration platform, and your internal comms strategy are essentially screaming into a void if people have checked out. After three decades watching companies throw tools at culture problems, I can tell you this: no software feature fixes what happens when people stop believing anyone's listening.

digital-culture.title: More companies like Microsoft are using buyouts. Should you take one?
digital-culture.excerpt: Microsoft is trying to cull its workforce by dangling an offer that might be hard for some employees to refuse. This week, the tech giant announced voluntary buyouts for 60,000 people, which is more t
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to over 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as a way to reduce headcount while letting people choose their own exit. Digital workplace pros need to understand this signals a broader trend where tech companies are using buyouts instead of layoffs, which affects recruiting, retention strategies, and how we talk about job security internally. The irony is calling mass departures a gift of "agency" to employees, which is corporate speak for "we need you gone but want you to feel good about it."

digital-culture.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
digital-culture.excerpt: Companies have spent the past several weeks trying to reassure investors that Muse and other AI agents pose more of an opportunity than a threat.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta released Muse, an AI agent designed to automate business tasks, and companies are scrambling to tell Wall Street it's a golden opportunity rather than a job killer. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because AI agents are moving from lab demos to actual deployment, which means real decisions about workflow automation are coming to your org whether you're ready or not. Here's the thing though: the fact that companies need to "reassure investors" tells you everything you need to know about whether people actually believe this is good news for workers.

industry-news.dwp_take: OnePlus just dropped two new phones with 9,000mAh batteries, active cooling systems, and 185Hz displays aimed squarely at mobile gamers. For digital workplace folks, this matters because your remote workforce is increasingly doing real work on high-performance phones, and all-day battery life plus thermal management actually enables productivity instead of killing it mid-Zoom call. Honestly, if your BYOD policy doesn't account for devices that can actually sustain a full workday without turning into a hand warmer, you're already behind.

industry-news.title: Dexcom G7 15-Day Glucose Monitor Launches in Canada in November
industry-news.excerpt: Dexcom G7 15 Day arrives in Canada in November with longer sensor wear and expanded insurance coverage. Here's what users should know before switching. The post Dexcom G7 15-Day Glucose Monitor Launch
industry-news.dwp_take: Dexcom's G7 glucose monitor is hitting the Canadian market in November with a longer 15-day wear cycle and better insurance coverage than previous versions. For digital workplace pros managing chronic conditions, this means fewer interruptions to your workday since you're changing sensors half as often. Look, I've covered workplace wellness tech for three decades, and every hour employees don't spend fiddling with medical devices is an hour they're actually working, which beats any ping-pong table in the break room.

industry-news.title: Google Unveils Gemini Suggested Autofill for Chrome: What Users Should Know
industry-news.excerpt: Google is adding Gemini-powered autofill to Chrome using information from Gmail. Learn how it works, who can use it, and what privacy concerns to consider. The post Google Unveils Gemini Suggested Aut
industry-news.dwp_take: Google is rolling out AI-powered autofill in Chrome that uses your Gmail data to suggest information when you're filling out forms online. This matters to digital workplace folks because it touches the third rail of enterprise security: what data gets shared between applications and how much AI systems are learning about your users. Here's the thing though, giving an AI system access to your email history to fill out web forms is like handing your diary to a chatbot and hoping it only reads the boring parts.

industry-news.title: This Week in Tech: Apple Gets Touchy as AI Clocks In
industry-news.excerpt: See what you missed in Daily Tech Insider from Oct. 26–30. The post This Week in Tech: Apple Gets Touchy as AI Clocks In appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple introduced new AI features and touchscreen capabilities to its devices this week while the broader tech industry continues rolling out workplace AI tools. Digital workplace leaders need to watch Apple's moves because their design philosophy and security standards often set the bar that enterprises eventually expect across all their platforms. Here's the thing though: most organizations are still struggling to get people to actually use their existing collaboration tools, so adding more AI features feels like buying someone a fancy espresso machine when they haven't finished their coffee from yesterday.
